Given the choices provided, none accurately describe the updates in GINA 2025 regarding asthma management based on available information up to my cut-off date (01 March 2023). However, I can provide an explanation for why certain options might be misleading or incorrect. A) This statement is inaccurate. The updated guidelines recommend that step-up therapy should include adding a long-acting beta2-adrenergic agonist (LABA) or inhaled corticosteroids to SABA as needed, not relying solely on SABA for mild asthma without any additional treatment when symptoms occur. B) This option is misleading because biologic therapies are recommended for patients with uncontrolled asthma despite having an appropriate controller medication that can be tolerated and well-tolerated according to the patient's preferences. It doesn't necessarily state all patients with persistent asthma, regardless of phenotype, should start these therapies without any further consideration. C) The combination of formoterol + inhaled corticosteroid is indeed recommended for maintenance treatment in mild to moderate asthma as per GINA 2025 guidelines. However, this option might be slightly misleading because the recommendation often includes that a LABA or an inhaled corticosteroid could also serve relief medication on an as-needed basis. D) Monitoring of lung function can continue even after patients have been stable for more than 12 months to ensure the asthma does not worsen and to monitor any changes. It is not recommended to stop monitoring entirely based solely on stability duration. E) The updated GINA 2025 did introduce a stepped treatment approach that considers the severity, frequency of symptoms, and patient preferences when deciding on the appropriate controller medication and reliever therapy for asthma management. This does not mean replacing the concept of a stepped approach with an absolute uniform model across all patients. Given these considerations, none of the options A through E accurately describe the GINA 2025 recommendations without significant inaccuracy or omission.

Statement A is true because regular use of inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) is a cornerstone treatment for moderate to severe persistent asthma in children, reducing airway inflammation and preventing exacerbations. Inhaled corticosteroids are effective in reducing symptoms, hospitalizations, and deaths from asthma. They work by decreasing inflammation in the airways, which can help reduce wheezing, coughing, and shortness of breath. The National Asthma Education and Prevention Program (NAEPP) and other reputable medical organizations recommend ICS as a first-line treatment for children with moderate to severe persistent asthma. However, it is essential to note that ICS should be used under the guidance of a healthcare provider, as they can have side effects and interact with other medications.

Mepolizumab is a monoclonal antibody that targets interleukin-5 (IL-5), which plays a key role in the growth and survival of eosinophils, making it effective in treating severe eosinophilic asthma. The Global Initiative for Asthma Management and Prevention (GINA) recommends mepolizumab as a biologic option for patients with severe asthma.

The most appropriate therapeutic approach for this patient is to combine Formoterol/Budesonide every 12 hours with Tiotropium 1x/day, and Salbutamol as needed. This combination provides a balanced control of inflammation, bronchospasm, and airflow limitation, which are all key components of asthma management. The addition of Tiotropium, an anticholinergic medication, will help to further reduce symptoms by reducing airway secretions and increasing ciliary clearance.

Omalizumab is indicated for moderate to severe persistent allergic asthma not adequately controlled with inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) therapy. However, the patient's medication regimen already includes an ICS (budesonide 400mcg), and adding omalizumab could potentially mask the true severity of asthma and reduce the effectiveness of the ICS. The correct alternative is to maintain medications as they are, and add benralizumab, which targets the IL-5 pathway and can be used in patients with severe persistent asthma who require additional therapy beyond ICS. This approach will help manage symptoms and reduce exacerbations without over-reliance on systemic corticosteroids.
